sections.heading: 1 · A Battery Cell in Sixty Seconds
bullets: Two units, one relationship: AMP-HOURS (Ah) measure how much electric charge a cell holds; WATT-HOURS (Wh) measure energy — and Wh = Ah × voltage. An LFP cell sits at ~3.2 V, so a 314 Ah cell stores ~1 kWh and a 1,175 Ah cell ~3.76 kWh. When a spec sheet says '587Ah cell,' multiply by 3.2 to know the energy.

LFP (lithium iron phosphate) is the chemistry of grid storage: cheaper materials (no nickel or cobalt), much harder to set on fire, and far more charge-discharge cycles than the nickel-based (NMC) chemistry EVs long used — its penalty is lower energy density (heavier per kWh). On a concrete pad, weight is nearly free. In a car, it isn't. That one difference explains why stationary storage diverged from EV batteries.

The number that actually prices grid storage is cost per delivered kWh over the battery's life ≈ price ÷ (usable energy × cycle count × efficiency). Energy density barely appears; CYCLE LIFE is a straight multiplier. A cell rated 13,000 cycles delivers roughly twice the lifetime energy of one rated 6,500 at the same price — that's why storage-cell spec sheets lead with cycles, not Wh/kg.

Degradation is the enemy being engineered against: every cycle wears the electrodes (cycle aging) and time itself degrades the chemistry (calendar aging). Health is tracked as SOH (state of health — remaining capacity vs new). 10,000+ cycles at one cycle per day is 27+ years — matching the 20–25-year life of the solar farm next door.

Round-trip efficiency (RTE): of every 100 kWh you charge in, only ~92–96 come back out; the rest becomes heat (wire resistance losses grow with the square of current — I²R). Lost energy is lost revenue twice: you bought it AND you must cool it away, which is why every tenth of a percent matters at the megawatt scale.

sections.heading: 2 · How Cells Become Grid Storage — the DC Block and the Value Chain
bullets: The assembly ladder: CELL (a prismatic can) → MODULE (cells welded into a serviceable brick) → RACK (modules stacked in series to reach ~1,300–1,500 V DC) → DC BLOCK (a 20-ft container of racks with liquid cooling, fire suppression, and a battery management system) → add a PCS (power conversion system — the big inverter) and a transformer, and you're on the grid.

Configuration notation decodes the ladder: '1P416S' means 416 cells in series (S), one parallel string (P). Series stacking adds voltage (416 × 3.2 V ≈ 1,330 V DC); parallel adds capacity. High DC voltage exists for the same reason the grid uses high voltage — halving current quarters the I²R wiring losses.

The DC BLOCK is the industry's LEGO brick: the cell maker ships an energy container; someone else typically adds the PCS, the site-level EMS (energy management system — the software deciding when to charge/discharge), and the construction. Selling DC blocks instead of bare cells captures more value per MWh without competing head-on with full-system integrators.

Who adds what value: the CELL MAKER turns chemistry into cans; the SYSTEM INTEGRATOR turns blocks + PCS + software into a plant; the EPC builds it; the DEVELOPER/IPP owns and monetizes it (energy arbitrage, capacity payments, grid services). One company can occupy several rungs — a cell maker that also sells DC blocks is both supplier to and competitor of integrators who buy its cells.

Two engineering facts shape every modern container: LIQUID COOLING replaced air because keeping every cell within a few degrees of its neighbors is what preserves cycle life (uneven temperature = uneven aging = weakest-cell limits); and THERMAL-RUNAWAY certification (UL 9540A large-scale fire testing, NFPA 855 siting rules) is the passport to Western markets — no test data, no project.

sections.heading: 3 · The Big-Cell Bet — What 280 → 587 → 1,175 Ah Changes
bullets: The format ladder in one line: 280 Ah (first-generation standard) → 314 Ah (today's volume workhorse) → 587 Ah (the emerging 500+ class) → 1,175 Ah and 1,300 Ah (kilo-amp-hour class, unique territory) — same chemistry, same container, radically fewer cells.

Why bigger cells matter structurally: a 5 MWh container needs ~5,000 cells at 314 Ah but only ~1,300 at 1,175 Ah — a ~70% cut in cells, welds, busbars, sensors, and BMS channels. Every eliminated connection is an eliminated failure point and an eliminated assembly cost. The physics enabler: storage discharges gently (2–8 hours), so a huge cell's thicker electrodes and slower heat removal are acceptable — an EV, which must dump energy in minutes, could never use one.

Why bigger cells matter economically: the project metric is MWh per 20-ft container — ~3.7 (280 Ah era) → 5.0 (314 Ah blocks) → 6.25 (587/1,175 Ah) → 6.9 (1,300 Ah). More energy per box = fewer containers, less land, less cabling, less installation labor per MWh. Cell-level density gains are modest (~20%), but rack/module-level gains from redesigning around big cells reach 60–80%.

The tradeoffs being engineered around: a bigger cell concentrates more energy in one failure unit (fire testing gets harder), loses more capacity if one cell dies, and needs ultra-thick electrodes manufactured without defects — which is why mass-producing a 1,175 Ah cell is a process achievement, not just a design choice, and why derivative formats (587 Ah cut from the 1,175 Ah platform) share one production platform.

The container family maps straight onto the cell ladder: standard 20-ft utility blocks (314 Ah → ∞Block 4.18/5.016 MWh; 587/1,175 Ah → 6.25 MWh 2h/4h), a 10-ft modular variant under 26 tonnes for crane- and road-constrained sites (Flexsso), cabinet-scale C&I units (261 kWh–1 MWh, the same big-cell logic shrunk — 1,175 Ah cells cut cabinet cell count ~70%), and consumer LFP products reusing the same long-life cells.

sections.heading: 4 · Long Duration and Sodium — Same Lens, New Variables
bullets: Power vs energy, the distinction everything hangs on: MW is how fast a plant can discharge, MWh is how much it holds; DURATION = MWh ÷ MW. A 2-hour battery chases price spikes and frequency services; a 4-hour battery shifts solar into the evening peak; 8-hour LDES (long-duration energy storage) carries renewables overnight — the segment regulators are now mandating (e.g. New South Wales requires 8-hour assets in its 28 GWh-by-2033 program).

'8-hour-native' vs 'stretched': you can make any battery last 8 hours by discharging it gently, but you're then paying for power hardware you never use. A native LDES design starts at the cell — a huge energy brick (1,300 Ah) discharged at 0.125P (one-eighth of capacity per hour), minimizing degradation and maximizing energy per container (6.9 MWh) — with the PCS sized small relative to storage. Duration becomes a design axis, not an afterthought.

LDES economics: at long durations the cost of power electronics amortizes over more delivered hours, so $/kWh of the cells dominates the project price — exactly the variable big cheap long-lived LFP (and eventually sodium) attacks. This is why the LDES race is a big-cell race.

Sodium-ion is the same playbook with a different element: swap lithium for sodium (from common salt — no lithium, cobalt, or nickel supply exposure), accept roughly half the energy density (~95 Wh/kg vs ~173+ for LFP), and gain extreme cycle life (≥20,000), -40 °C cold tolerance, and immunity to lithium price swings. On a concrete pad, density again barely matters — sodium's real contest with LFP is purely $/kWh-cycle.

Where sodium fits today: high-cycling short-duration work (frequency regulation — a 2.28 MWh 1-hour container class), brutally cold climates, and as a strategic hedge; it stays niche while lithium is cheap, and becomes a volume product the moment lithium isn't.

sections.heading: 5 · Industry Map — Who Buys, Who Competes, Why a Specialist Exists
bullets: Who buys, at three levels: INTEGRATORS and OEMs buy bare cells to build their own systems; DEVELOPERS, EPCs, and UTILITIES buy DC blocks for utility projects (grid tenders, LDES mandates, reconstruction programs); DISTRIBUTORS and installers buy C&I cabinets and home units. A cell-plus-block vendor serves all three — and its cell customers (integrators) compete with its block business, a structural tension of the dual model.

The competitive field: in storage cells the giants are CATL (global #1, diversified across EV + storage), EVE, BYD, and REPT — all of whom split attention and capacity with EV batteries. In systems, integrators like Tesla, Sungrow, and Fluence buy or make cells and add PCS + software. The current technical frontier is the large-format race: 587 Ah-class cells (CATL, EVE's 628 Ah, Hithium) are becoming the standard, with the kAh class (1,175/1,300 Ah) so far a one-player tier.

Why a stationary-only specialist can exist: focus buys three advantages — cell design optimized purely for cycle life and $/kWh (no EV compromise on density), no allocation conflict when EV demand spikes (a diversified giant feeds its car customers first), and a product roadmap (bigger cells, longer durations, sodium) that tracks grid economics rather than automotive fashion. The bet: storage is becoming its own industry, not EV's side market.

Geography is product strategy now: rising US tariffs on Chinese battery imports (7% → 26% in 2026) and EU battery regulations make local assembly a selling point — hence US module/system assembly in Texas, planned European cell production in Spain, and 'EU Battery Regulation-aligned' as a product feature. Even technology licensing is geopolitics: China's export controls on battery technology can veto deals (as India's Reliance discovered when its licensing plan collapsed in 2026).

How to read any storage-supplier announcement: identify the layer (cell, block, or full system?), the duration (2h merchant, 4h solar-shifting, 8h mandate-driven?), the cell format (314 Ah commodity or large-format?), and the localization angle (where is it assembled, whose tariffs does it dodge?). Those four questions place any product or deal in this industry within seconds.

flashcards.q: A cell is rated 314 Ah at 3.2 V. Roughly how much energy does it store, and what's the difference between Ah and Wh?
flashcards.a: Ah measures charge; Wh measures energy; Wh = Ah × V. So 314 Ah × 3.2 V ≈ 1,000 Wh = ~1 kWh. A 1,175 Ah cell at the same voltage stores ~3.76 kWh.

flashcards.q: Why do stationary-storage cells optimize cycle life and cost instead of energy density?
flashcards.a: Lifetime economics ≈ price ÷ (usable energy × cycles × efficiency). On a concrete pad, weight and volume are nearly free, so Wh/kg barely matters — but cycle count multiplies lifetime energy delivered directly. Double the cycles ≈ half the cost per delivered kWh.

flashcards.q: Why is LFP the chemistry of grid storage rather than the nickel-based (NMC) chemistry EVs used?
flashcards.a: LFP is cheaper (no nickel/cobalt), much more fire-resistant, and lasts far more cycles; its penalty — lower energy density — matters in a car but not in a container. Grid storage trades density it doesn't need for cost, safety, and longevity it does.

flashcards.q: What is a DC block, and what does a system integrator add to it?
flashcards.a: A DC block is a factory-built container of racks with liquid cooling, fire suppression, and a BMS — energy only, no AC output. The integrator adds the PCS (the big inverter), transformer, and EMS software, turning stored DC energy into a dispatchable grid plant.

flashcards.q: Decode '1P416S' — and why do racks stack cells to ~1,300–1,500 V DC?
flashcards.a: 416 cells in series (S) × 1 parallel string (P). Series adds voltage: 416 × 3.2 V ≈ 1,330 V. High voltage means low current for the same power, and wiring losses scale with current squared (I²R) — so high-voltage DC cuts copper and losses.

flashcards.q: What changes structurally when you build a container from 1,175 Ah cells instead of 314 Ah cells?
flashcards.a: About 70% fewer cells — so ~70% fewer welds, busbars, sensors, and BMS channels. Every eliminated connection is an eliminated failure point and assembly cost, and module/rack-level energy density gains reach 60–80% when the system is redesigned around the big cell.

flashcards.q: Why can grid storage use kilo-amp-hour cells (1,175–1,300 Ah) when EVs never could?
flashcards.a: Discharge rate. Storage drains over 2–8 hours (as low as 0.125P), so thick electrodes and slow heat removal are fine. An EV must deliver huge bursts and fast charges — a giant thick-electrode cell can't shed heat fast enough for that duty.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between MW and MWh, and what does 'duration' mean?
flashcards.a: MW is discharge speed (power); MWh is the amount stored (energy); duration = MWh ÷ MW. A 100 MW / 400 MWh plant is a '4-hour' battery — it can hold its full power output for four hours.

flashcards.q: What makes a storage system '8-hour-native' rather than a stretched 4-hour product?
flashcards.a: The design starts at the cell: a very large energy-optimized cell discharged at ~0.125P, with power electronics sized small relative to storage. You avoid paying for power hardware you never use, minimize degradation, and maximize MWh per container — duration as a design axis, not a derating.

flashcards.q: Why does cell cost ($/kWh) dominate long-duration storage economics more than in short-duration systems?
flashcards.a: The PCS and grid hardware are sized to power (MW), which stays fixed while energy (MWh) grows with duration — so at 8 hours their cost amortizes over 4× the energy of a 2-hour system. What's left of the price is mostly cells, which is why the LDES race is a cheap-big-cell race.

flashcards.q: What does sodium-ion trade away, and what does it gain over LFP for grid use?
flashcards.a: It gives up roughly half the energy density (~95 vs ~173+ Wh/kg). In exchange: no lithium/cobalt/nickel exposure (sodium comes from common salt), extreme cycle life (≥20,000), -40 °C operation, and price stability. On a concrete pad the density loss barely matters — the contest is purely $/kWh-cycle.

flashcards.q: What are cycle aging, calendar aging, and SOH — and why does 10,000+ cycles matter?
flashcards.a: Cycle aging is wear from each charge-discharge; calendar aging is chemical decay over time regardless of use; SOH (state of health) is remaining capacity vs new. At one cycle/day, 10,000+ cycles is 27+ years — letting the battery live as long as the solar or wind plant beside it.

flashcards.q: Why did BESS containers move from air to liquid cooling?
flashcards.a: Cycle life depends on every cell aging evenly; a pack degrades at the rate of its hottest cell. Liquid cooling holds all cells within a few degrees of each other, preserving uniformity — and removes heat densely enough for today's 5–7 MWh containers, which air physically can't.

flashcards.q: Why can a stationary-only cell specialist survive against diversified giants like CATL or BYD?
flashcards.a: Focus: cell designs optimized purely for cycle life and $/kWh with no EV compromises; no allocation conflict when EV demand spikes (diversified makers feed car customers first); and a roadmap (bigger cells, longer duration, sodium) that tracks grid economics rather than automotive needs.

flashcards.q: Why do storage suppliers build assembly plants in the US and cell plants in Europe instead of exporting everything from China?
flashcards.a: Tariffs and content rules: US tariffs on Chinese battery products rose from 7% to 26% in 2026, and EU battery regulation rewards local, compliant production. Local assembly converts a trade barrier into a selling point — and even technology licensing can be blocked by China's export controls, closing that alternative channel.
